More light at night was associated with subtle differences in the heart’s structure and ability to contract, even in adults without diagnosed cardiovascular disease.

Compared with no nighttime exposure, high exposure (about 34 minutes per night) was associated with thicker walls and greater muscle mass in the heart’s main pumping chamber, along with poorer measures of contraction.

High exposure was also associated with a 15-33% higher risk of heart failure, heart attack, stroke, Afib, and cardiovascular death in a larger follow-up analysis.

Light is a biological signal, and evening light can suppress melatonin and shift our circadian clocks later, affecting systems that regulate sleep and cardiovascular function.

I’ve previously shared how I programmed my home lighting to turn red in the evening and used blackout curtains in our bedrooms to support sleep.

So to me, this study is yet another reason to take nighttime light seriously. Bright days, dim evenings, and dark bedrooms are practical ways to support our circadian rhythms (and our heart health!)

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Brand new study just dropped (published Oct 29, 2026 in Frontiers in Pharmacology). 
A massive new analysis from two of the world’s largest biomedical databases just linked statin use to roughly double the risk of dementia.

Researchers looked at the All of Us Research Program (83,355 adults, including over 31,000 statin users, followed through 2023) and the UK Biobank (173,282 adults, including nearly 44,000 statin users). After balancing groups for age, BMI, APOE status, comorbidities, and other factors using inverse probability of treatment weighting, statin users showed adjusted hazard ratios of 2.22 (All of Us) and 2.54 (UK Biobank) for incident dementia.

The association held across Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, and other subtypes. High-intensity statins carried an additional ~14% higher risk compared with moderate-to-low intensity therapy. Incidence rates were higher in the discovery cohort (64.9 vs 30.7 per 10,000 person-years) than in the replication cohort, but the relative increase was consistent.

In an exploratory mediation analysis, a modest portion (8.2%) of the association appeared to run through lower levels of coenzyme Q7—a protein involved in CoQ10 biosynthesis. Lower COQ7 was itself linked to higher dementia odds. The pathway through LDL-C was not statistically significant. The authors note this is hypothesis-generating and that direct CoQ10 was not measured.

This is observational data, not a randomized trial, so it cannot prove causation. Residual confounding (including why people were prescribed statins) remains possible, and the literature on statins and cognition has been mixed. Still, the scale, the replication across two independent cohorts, the intensity-dependent pattern, and the COQ7 signal make it hard to ignore.

This is the kind of result that makes people who have been skeptical of long-term statin use for primary prevention sit up and take notice—especially given the CoQ10 connection many clinicians have quietly acknowledged for years.

The full paper is open access: https://t.co/dEanGT17LV

Dr. Hyman is right, and the data behind it is old enough that every doctor should know it by now. Blood sugar is the last thing to break.

The Whitehall II study followed 6,538 British civil servants who did not have diabetes, for a median of 9.7 years. 505 of them got diabetes, and the researchers went back and tracked what their labs did before the diagnosis.

Fasting glucose crept up slowly, then rose steeply starting 3 years before diagnosis, from 5.79 to 7.40 mmol/L. That is about 104 to 133 mg/dL. Insulin sensitivity fell steeply during the 5 years before diagnosis. Beta-cell output actually rose between years 4 and 3 before diagnosis, then fell.

The authors wrote that they saw "changes in glucose concentrations, insulin sensitivity, and insulin secretion as much as 3-6 years before diagnosis of diabetes."

So the pancreas was working overtime for years while the standard glucose number still looked fine. That is hyperinsulinemia, and few doctors ever check for it. A fasting glucose by itself is the late warning.

Ask your doctor for a fasting insulin test. If it is high, Low-carb/Keto/Carnivore is how you bring it down.

You've been told high cholesterol will put you in an early grave. A Swedish study of 44,636 people found the ones who lived to 100 had higher cholesterol. Why? Read on...

Researchers in Sweden drew blood on 44,636 people aged 64 to 99 and followed them for up to 35 years. 1,224 of them lived to see their 100th birthday.

The people who made it to 100 had higher total cholesterol and higher iron. They had lower glucose, lower creatinine, and lower uric acid.

The authors wrote that the cholesterol finding "stands in contrast to clinical guidelines regarding cholesterol levels." Those are their words, not mine.

This was an observational study, so it can't prove cholesterol made anybody live longer. But it does not fit the story that higher cholesterol means you die young. The number that pointed the wrong way was blood sugar. Few doctors check for hyperinsulinemia, so ask your doctor for a fasting insulin test.

She was introverted, dealt with asthma, and had a herniated disc. Then came the breast cancer diagnosis.

Surgery and treatment followed. Doctors suggested she do “some light exercise.” That simple advice became the turning point. Chao started going to the gym. She noticed something immediate: at home she felt drained; around the weights, energy returned. For the first time in her life, she found something she genuinely wanted to do.

She trained consistently. What began as recovery became purpose. She eventually became a certified fitness coach and now starts her days at 4 a.m., riding an electric bike to the gym, training small muscle groups and doing cardio before coaching clients from morning until night. In her gym in Kunshan she is the oldest coach—and one of the most noticed.

In 1953 a Harvard nutritionist named Jean Mayer proposed that hunger is not driven by how much glucose is in the blood, but by how much glucose the brain is able to use.

He called it the glucostatic theory.

The idea was simple. Specialized cells in the hypothalamus act as glucose sensors. When those cells are taking up and using plenty of glucose, a person feels full. When glucose use falls, a person feels hungry and starts looking for food.

Mayer's key point was that the absolute level of blood glucose is not the signal. The signal is glucose utilization. He estimated it from the arteriovenous difference, which is the gap between glucose in the arteries going into the tissues and glucose in the veins coming out of them.

This explained something that bothered physicians at the time. People with poorly controlled diabetes often have very high blood glucose and are still constantly hungry. Without enough insulin, their cells cannot take the glucose in. The blood is full of fuel, but the tissues are using very little of it.

Mayer published the idea in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1953. In 1955 he expanded it, and he placed it next to a second idea, the lipostatic hypothesis. That hypothesis held that the body also tracks how much fat it carries over the long term.

That pairing turned out to be important.

Over the following decades the glucostatic theory was shown to be incomplete:
- Hunger is controlled by many signals, not one.
- Gut hormones, stomach stretch, learned meal times, and reward all play a role.
- The discovery of leptin in the 1990s confirmed that fat tissue signals the brain about long-term energy stores, which is much closer to Mayer's lipostatic idea.

But the glucose part of the story never went away. Modern measurement methods brought it back.

Campfield and colleagues, 1996:
- 18 healthy adults were isolated from food and time cues, with blood glucose monitored continuously.
- In 83% of them, rising hunger and spoken meal requests were preceded by a brief drop in blood glucose.
- The average low point was about 10% below baseline, reached around 27 minutes into the drop.
- In a small preliminary arm, insulin was infused to mimic these drops, and hunger ratings rose. When glucose stayed stable, hunger did not change.

Melanson and colleagues, 1999:
- Time-blinded men who drank a high-fat or a sugar drink requested their next meal during the decline in glucose that followed the post-drink peak.
- After the fat drink, the next meal request took about twice as long (126 vs 65 minutes).

Lennerz and colleagues, 2013:
- 12 men ate a high-glycemic or low-glycemic meal matched for calories, macronutrients, and taste.
- The high-glycemic meal produced 2.4 times more glucose in the first 2 hours.
- 4 hours later, glucose was lower after the high-glycemic meal (4.7 vs 5.3 mmol/L) and hunger was higher.
- At that point, brain imaging showed greater activity in the nucleus accumbens, a region tied to reward and craving.

Wyatt and colleagues, 2021:
- 1,070 people wore continuous glucose monitors across 8,624 standardized meals.
- The size of the glucose dip 2 to 3 hours after a meal predicted hunger better than the size of the glucose peak.
- Bigger dips were linked to a shorter time until the next meal, more energy eaten 3 to 4 hours later, and more energy eaten over 24 hours.

These studies show the same pattern. The rise in glucose is not what drives the next round of hunger. The fall is.

That is where insulin comes in.

A large glucose spike brings a large insulin response. Insulin moves glucose out of the blood and into tissues, and when the response is large it can push glucose below where it started. That drop is the dip. The insulin infusions in Campfield's work produced the same kind of drop and the same rise in hunger.

Mayer had the right instinct. The brain pays close attention to glucose, and the timing and direction of glucose changes after a meal shape when people eat next and how much. He was wrong only in thinking it was the whole story.

The hormone that controls those changes is insulin. If the goal is to control hunger after a meal, it's clear that meals which avoid a large glucose spike, and the large insulin response that follows it, are the more reliable way to avoid the dip that drives a person to eat again.

Calories in, calories out has merit (energy needs to be accounted for), but its main flaw is that it's hard to fully account for the calories, especially the ones going out. There's a study I come back to that shows this better than any other.

In 1999, researchers at the Mayo Clinic took 16 healthy, non-obese adults and overfed every one of them by exactly 1,000 calories a day for eight weeks. Same surplus, same duration, carefully controlled. If body fat were simple arithmetic, everyone should have gained roughly the same amount of fat.

They didn't. Fat gain ranged from less than half a kilogram to more than four kilograms. That's about a tenfold difference between people eating the same extra food.

The researchers measured where the extra energy went. Resting metabolism barely changed. The energy spent digesting food rose a little, about the same in everyone. Formal exercise was held constant, because the volunteers weren't allowed to start working out.

The big difference was in what they called non-exercise activity thermogenesis, or NEAT. This is the energy spent on everything that isn't deliberate exercise: standing, shifting in a chair, fidgeting, walking around the house, staying on one's feet instead of sitting.

When overfed, some people automatically increased this everyday movement by nearly 700 calories a day. Others didn't increase it at all, and a few actually moved less. Nobody told them to do this, and most probably had no idea it was happening.

The change in NEAT was the strongest predictor of who gained fat and who didn't. The people whose daily movement rose the most stored the least fat, and the people whose movement didn't budge stored the most.

What I find most interesting is that this is something the body does on its own. It has a built-in way to defend against a calorie surplus, and it works much better in some people than in others. That helps explain why two people can eat similar diets and end up with very different bodies.

It's also changed how I think about my own day. An hour at the gym is only a small slice of it. The other 15 or so waking hours, and how much of them a person spends sitting, add up to far more energy than most workouts.

If the goal is controlling body fat, it's clear that the movement a person does outside the gym deserves as much attention as the workout itself.

In a quiet lab at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, psychologist Robert Sorge and his team set out to test something that defied the usual medical script for knee osteoarthritis: instead of more pills or surgery, could the food on the plate itself turn down the pain? 

Knee OA is the most common form of arthritis—roughly 15% of Americans deal with it, and the grinding pain in weight-bearing joints often steals mobility and quality of life. Standard treatments (NSAIDs, opioids, injections) bring side effects that can cascade into more medications. Sorge, director of UAB’s PAIN Collective, hypothesized that refined carbohydrates were fueling oxidative stress and inflammation in ways that amplified functional pain—the kind that makes standing, walking, or climbing stairs feel punishing. A low-fat approach (the long-standing dietary default) might not be the answer.

The Experiment
In a randomized controlled pilot study published in Pain Medicine (2019/2020), 21 adults aged 65–75 (9 men, 12 women) with knee OA were assigned for 12 weeks to one of three paths: a low-carbohydrate diet (LCD), a low-fat diet (LFD), or continuing their usual eating (control). 

The LCD group started by dropping total (not just net) carbs to about ≤20 g/day for the first three weeks, then up to ≤40 g if needed. Protein and fat were unrestricted—think meats, eggs, limited non-starchy vegetables, nuts, seeds, butter, and oils. No calorie counting focused on weight loss alone. The low-fat group followed conventional lower-fat guidance. Every three weeks, the team measured self-reported pain, quality of life, and depression. They also tracked functional pain with real-world tasks: repeated chair stands, timed walks, and repeated knee stimulation to measure how much pain the movements themselves provoked. Blood was drawn before and after to check oxidative stress markers and the adipokine leptin.

What Happened
Both the low-carb and low-fat groups lost weight and BMI, as expected. But only the low-carb group showed clear, significant drops in pain intensity and unpleasantness during the functional tasks, plus better self-reported pain scores and quality-of-life improvements. The low-fat and usual-diet groups did not match those gains. The LCD also uniquely lowered oxidative stress and leptin levels; the drop in oxidative stress tracked with reduced functional pain. 
Sorge put it plainly: “Our work shows people can reduce their pain with a change in diet.” He added that weight loss alone did not explain the relief—“the quality of the diet and types of foods consumed have more to do with pain reduction than weight loss.” Diet would not “cure” the arthritis, but it could dial pain down so it no longer wrecked daily life, without the side-effect spiral of drugs. 

The Takeaway
It was a small pilot (21 people), so larger trials have followed, including work exploring diverse populations and comparing low-carb approaches to USDA-style diets. But the core finding landed: for these older adults with knee OA, cutting refined carbohydrates outperformed cutting fat on the measures that mattered most for living with the pain. The mechanism pointed toward lower oxidative stress and inflammation rather than the scale alone.
The story is a reminder that sometimes the most direct path to quieter joints is not another prescription—it’s what ends up on the plate.

So much time and money is spent trying to live longer, but what if one of the biggest levers is a hormone most people never think about?

People are paying for plasma transfusions and taking all kinds of bizarre drugs. Meanwhile, insulin gets very little attention in the longevity conversation, even though the evidence linking it to lifespan is strong.

This is one of the studies that changed how I think about aging. In 2017, Templeman and colleagues published a study in Cell Reports using mice with reduced insulin gene dosage. These mice had 25 to 34% lower circulating insulin. Their IGF-1 levels did not change. In old age, they had lower fasting glucose and better insulin sensitivity. And they lived longer, on two different diets. This was in mice, but it showed that lowering insulin itself can extend lifespan.

The human evidence points the same direction. In the Leiden Longevity Study, the middle-aged offspring of long-lived nonagenarian siblings had lower non-fasted glucose than their partners, with similar insulin and IGF-1 levels. When researchers measured insulin sensitivity directly, the offspring were more insulin sensitive than controls, and the more insulin sensitive they were, the longer their parents had lived.

Centenarians show this too. In 1996, Paolisso and colleagues found that healthy centenarians were more insulin sensitive than people over 75, and about as insulin sensitive as adults under 50. Their insulin action was preserved.

Long-lived families are typified by insulin sensitivity. If someone wants to age with a healthier metabolism, it's clear that keeping insulin low and insulin sensitivity high deserves a central place in the plan.
